claims.text: The starting material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 with an FCC matrix.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by synergistic elemental-composition effects.
Interactions among Al, Cr, and Ti are specifically responsible for governing degradation.
The interaction among Al, Cr, and Ti influences formation of a protective oxide layer.
The interaction among Al, Cr, and Ti influences stability of the FCC matrix.
A protective oxide layer forms during elevated-temperature gas exposure.
The proposed gas environments are air, nitrogen, and hydrogen.
The degradation rate will decrease by 20% relative to the starting-state baseline.
Oxidation-layer thickness will decrease by 15% relative to the starting-state baseline.
Elevated-temperature exposure will produce measurable microstructural changes relative to the starting state.
Comparing the starting alloy with a composition-modified variant under oxidizing and reducing gas exposure can test the proposed compositional mechanism.
A degradation-rate difference of less than 5% between the variant and baseline alloy would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The quantified 20% and 15% changes are stated relative to the as-manufactured starting-state baseline, whereas the experiment actually compares an exposed composition-modified variant with an exposed baseline alloy. An unexposed starting state does not itself define an exposure degradation rate or oxidation-layer thickness, so the stated comparison basis is internally inconsistent with the experimental design.
